candidates.title: Launch Preview: Falcon 9 and Chang Zheng rockets set to launch this week
candidates.raw_excerpt: Five orbital launches are scheduled worldwide for this week. In China, a Chang Zheng 6A and Chang Zheng 7A are set to launch two unknown payloads into orbit. Meanwhile, SpaceX has three Falcon 9 launches on the manifest from Florida and California, with two Starlink missions and a classified mission for the National Reconnaissance Office. Chang Zheng 7A | Unknown Payload The first launch of the week is a Chang Zheng 7A, scheduled to launch on Wednesday, July 29, from Launch Complex 201 (LC-201) at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China. The three-stage vehicle will launch within a one-hour, 57-minute launch window beginning at 11:42 UTC. The rocket is expected to follow an easterly trajectory to an unknown orbit. The 60.13-m-tall Chang Zheng 7A, developed by the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), is a three-stage medium-lift launch vehicle. The rocket has four liquid-fueled boosters fueled by kerosene (RP-1) and liquid oxygen (LOX). The first stage features two YF-100 oxidizer-rich staged combustion cycle engines fueled by RP-1 and LOX, while the second stage has four YF-115 engines also powered by RP-1 and LOX. An optional stage is also available, which features two YF-75 gas-generator-cycle engines powered by liquid hydrogen (LH2) and LOX. The rocket can carry up to 12,000 kg to low-Earth orbit (LEO) and has a liftoff thrust of 7,128 kN. This mission will be Chang Zheng 7A’s 17th launch and third mission of 2026. A Chang Zheng 6A launches from Taiyuan. (Credit: CASC) Chang Zheng 6A | Unknown Payload The second international launch of the week is a Chang Zheng 6A from Launch Complex 9A (LC-9A) at Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in China on Thursday, July 30. candidates.title: Rocket Lab to start launching missile-defense missions from Alaska under $266 million Space Force deal
candidates.raw_excerpt: Rocket Lab is expanding its launch operations to the snowy north. The California-based company, which already flies from New Zealand and Virginia, just inked a $266 million deal with the U.S. Space Force to fly up to 18 missile-defense missions , most of them from Alaska. "The size and scale of this contract reflects the Space Force's confidence in our ability to meet their urgent national security demands with speed, responsiveness and scale, and we're proud to provide the high-frequency launch capacity required to keep the U.S. ahead of global threats," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said in a statement today (July 27). The contract covers 12 suborbital launches, with the possibility of up to six more. These missions "will primarily take place" from the Pacific Spaceport Complex , a picturesque site on Alaska's Kodiak Island, which is most famous for its thriving population of brown bears. The spaceport has hosted nearly three dozen missions since opening in 1998, most of them suborbital flights for the U.S. military. Recently, however, it has supported launches of private orbital rockets — specifically, those built by Astra and ABL Space Systems (now known as Long Wall). The newly announced Rocket Lab missions will almost certainly be performed by HASTE , a suborbital variant of the company's workhorse Electron small-satellite launcher that customers use to test hypersonic technologies in the flight environment. They may also be part of the United States' sprawling Golden Dome missile-defense initiative, though we don't know that for sure; today's release provides few details about the launches. A Rocket Lab HASTE suborbital rocket launches on the "Prometheus Run" mission for the U.S. military on Nov. 18, 2025. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) Rocket Lab's primary launch site is on Māhia Peninsula, on the North Island of Peter Beck's native New Zealand. At the commissioners’ request, four police officers then swarmed Claridge, who challenged them to “drag me out,” which they did after placing the physics teacher in handcuffs. candidates.title: Experts warn current Starship heat shield tech is a "dead end" for rapid reuse
candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX successfully launched its Starship vehicle on Friday and appeared to demonstrate important and credible steps toward fulfilling the massive rocket's immense promise. As soon as the vehicle's next flight, Starship could go orbital, begin delivering satellites into space, and potentially return to the launch site to be 'caught' by the tower. All of this is impressive engineering on a gigantic scale. But despite the marked progress with the 13th test flight of Starship, one key issue—probably the key issue when it comes to Starship's future—remains unresolved. This concerns Starship's heat shield, the roughly 18,000 ceramic tiles that protect the vehicle's underbelly during its fiery return through Earth's atmosphere. And some experts say SpaceX's current approach may not get Starship to its ultimate goal of flying frequently, at low cost. Read full article Comments

candidates.title: SpaceX Stock Hammered After Starship Booster Fails in First Launch Since IPO
candidates.raw_excerpt: Was SpaceX’s recent Starship flight test a success or a failure? Many are hailing it as a victory, but several of the megarocket’s booster’s engines failed after re-entry, causing it to explode. SpaceX has had many similarly ambiguous tests before. But this was the first one since its much-hyped IPO earlier this summer — and it’s already clear that it wasn’t a convincing enough display to reverse the company’s fortunes on the stock market. After hitting an all time low before the weekend and closing at $115, SpaceX shares endeavored to plummet even further on Monday, briefly dipping to $108.66 — a new nadir since going public — before stabilizing around $110. The new low is over 20 percent below its opening IPO price of $135, and less than half of its all time high of more than $225 per share. It’s a sign of the scrutiny the company will be put through now that it’s a public entity , and comes despite certain predictions that a successful flight would help buoy the company’s shares. When Starship ran into trouble in the past, SpaceX mainly had to weather a storm of media coverage. Now, nervous investors represent yet another liability. “One of the benefits of being private is that there wasn’t a market to weigh in on and evaluate business decisions,” David Meier, senior investment analyst at the Motley Fool , told The Washington Post . “Being publicly traded means everything will be evaluated and information transmitted through market prices,” he added. “So every SpaceX launch, every Starlink decision and every xAI decision will be scrutinized by the market.” Spaceflight, at least currently, isn’t an ideal match for the make-a-quick-buck capitalism that Musk extolls. SpaceX has never been profitable, losing $5 billion last year alone. As Starship’s woes illustrate, rocket development is messy and complicated; there’s no guarantee that progress will be linear, if there’s any made at all. candidates.title: Sam Altman Announces That the Singularity Has Arrived
candidates.raw_excerpt: The “singularity” is here — according to Sam Altman, who we’d wager has an ulterior motive behind promoting this claim. The OpenAI CEO harbingered this sea-changing paradigm shift on a podcast over the weekend. “We are now, like, in the singularity,” Altman said on the latest episode of “Relentless,” as spotted by Business Insider . Definitions vary, but the singularity is generally defined as the moment that the capabilities of thinking machines might start to accelerate at a pace beyond humankind’s control, possibly leading to the creation of a powerful superintelligence. Whether that’s actually happening right now is dubious. But Altman has a lot tied up in hyping the idea, and he’s been doing it for a long time. In a blog post titled “The Gentle Singularity” published almost exactly a year ago, he claimed humankind is “past the event horizon; the takeoff has started,” saying we were close to building the much-vaunted superintelligence. “Now we’re actually in the moment that we used to talk about at the lunch table in a very not-serious way,” Altman said on the podcast. “I’ve been waiting for this my whole life, and I think it’s going to be incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world.” Altman’s comments come days after OpenAI claimed that several of its AI models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and, mysteriously, an “even more capable pre-release model,” broke out of their research environment, gained access to the internet, and hacked their way into a database to find the answers for cybersecurity tests. Hugging Face, the open source AI platform whose database the AIs raided, confirmed it had  been hit with an intrusion “run by an autonomous agent framework executing many thousands of individual actions.” Ostensibly, this was an urgent warning shot of how powerful AI systems have become. candidates.title: A Whole Bunch of People’s Claude Chats Are Publicly Accessible Online, and There’s Some Wildly Private Stuff in There
candidates.raw_excerpt: A trove of chat logs and projects created with Anthropic’s Claude — some including sensitive personal and company information — have been left exposed to Google, making them them searchable to anyone on the web. Many of the materials appear to have been made public when Claude users opted to distribute a given chat or project to colleagues or associates using the chatbot’s “share” feature. After hitting the “share” button in the top right corner, Claude notes that sharing will create a “public” link, which “anyone with the link can view.” The warning, though, doesn’t alert users that shared content could wind up being indexed by a search engine — meaning that a user could effectively be sharing their Claude-generated document with the entire internet. Other materials were shared in the form of Claude Artifacts, a feature that allows users to save certain projects as standalone apps or tools. That platform does warn users that publishing an Artifact “will make it accessible to anyone on the internet and potentially visible in search engine results.” Some of the materials exposed to the web and indexed by Google, such as personal websites and some vibe-coded apps, appear to have been created for public consumption. But much of the discoverable content seems as though it was only intended to be shared internally at a company, or between a small handful of people. Such documents, which were reviewed by Futurism by way of Google Search, included what appeared to be a detailed medical report of a real patient, clinical trial results that included patient names, documents sharing the names and phone numbers of primary school-aged children, company documents marked for internal use only, and employee reviews that included personal information about workers. (We’re opting not to share any links to the content out of concern for users’ privacy.) The exposure was first spotted by Redditors over the weekend. As of today, the chats remain searchable. candidates.title: The AI Industry Has Acted So Badly That It’s Now Dealing With a Huge Wave of Hatred
candidates.raw_excerpt: The tech overlords pushing the AI boom are quickly wearing out what little welcome they had. You may have noticed big-name AI labs pushing new commercials lately. Meta’s new 60-second ad spot insists that the “future is for everyone,” even as CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s personal net worth eclipses the GDP of Hungary. Anthropic’s new commercial for Claude assures viewers that there’s “hope in hard questions,” seemingly embracing the discomfort that comes when your software is used to bomb elementary schools in Iran. For as magnanimous as these new PR stunts appear on the surface, a vast swathe of the public they’re meant to sway are rejecting the industry’s faux-populism messaging out of hand, as the cost of AI — born out in inflation , data center pollution , fears of job loss and mental health concerns — becomes too much to bear. According to data compiled by Pew Research , 40 percent of US adults predict AI will have a negative impact on society writ large, compared to just 16 percent who say it’ll have a positive effect. A whole 31 percent of those surveyed think AI will have negative consequences for themselves, personally, over the next 20 years. As disgust with AI itself grows, so too does resistance to the hardware embodying its rise. Per a separate poll by Gallup , flagged by Business Insider , an astonishing three-quarters of US adults are now resolutely opposed to hyperscale data centers popping up near their home. City councils are increasingly forced to reconcile with landowners hostile to any AI data center appearing in their district, putting significant strain on developers hoping to gorge themselves on the fruits of the AI boom. Protests against AI companies are flaring up across the country, with Time reporting 142 protests across 42 states in one day alone. Beyond data centers, a decentralized but highly-motivated movement is growing around the chopping, hacking, and outright sabotage of AI-integrated surveillance cameras . candidates.title: The Type of Orbital Data Centers That Billionaires Want to Launch Into Space Would Wreak Ecological Catastrophe, Scientists Warn
candidates.raw_excerpt: Over the past year or so, a puzzling idea has taken hold among billionaires ranging from Elon Musk to Jeff Bezos: that instead of trying to force data centers on communities that don’t want them down on Earth, it would be much easier just to launch them into space. The economics and logistics of the scheme, many experts have pointed out, are absolutely absurd. And even beyond those practical concerns, if corporations actually did somehow manage to fill the planet’s orbit with the facilities, scientists are now warning that the environmental cost would be devastating. A new petition organized by the group EarthJustice, first reported by the Guardian , is warning of “catastrophic” consequences for the planet if the billionaire-backed dream ever came to pass. The 29-page petition calls on the US Federal Communications Commission to investigate current orbital data center licensing requests as potentially in violation of “federal law,” joining the chorus of experts warning that it’s a horrible idea for just about everybody. “The FCC is currently considering multiple requests for licensing extraordinary numbers of satellite-based data centers to be placed into low-earth orbit over the next decade,” the petition begins. “The proponents of these proposals describe their plans in grandiose, civilization-changing terms. But these same proponents have refused to embrace any inquiry into the impacts of their self claimed epochal technology on the environment, science, economy, or other values. This is not just poor planning and a missed opportunity: it violates federal law.” The filing does double duty. On top of formally petitioning the FCC to prepare an environmental assessment , it’s also a “petition to deny,” which is a legal mechanism that requires the petitioner to back up their claims with verified facts. candidates.title: ESA Ground Station in Spain Cleared to Return to Service After Wildfire Threat
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: ESA The European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher announced on 26 July that the agency had cleared its Cebreros deep-space ground station in Spain to return to service after inspections confirmed that the facility escaped damage from wildfires. Aschbacher explained that teams had completed the necessary checks and tests at the Cebreros station and cleared its 35-metre antenna to resume nominal operations from 27 July. “After careful review, we have declared the antenna GREEN for nominal operations as of 27 July,” said Aschbacher. He added that any on-site presence would be kept to a minimum in accordance with restrictions that remain in force in the area. The threat to the station was part of a wider wildfire emergency that began several days earlier. On Thursday 23 July, the Spanish government declared a national emergency as several large fires spread through the province of Ávila and neighbouring Madrid. The announcement stated that the wildfires had created a “particularly serious situation” due to their rapid spread and impact on inhabited areas. On 24 July, images began to emerge showing wildfires approaching ESA’s Cebreros ground station, with an evacuation order forcing staff to leave the site. In a 25 July update, ESA said that wildfires had come “very close” to the station. At the time, the agency explained that it appeared to have escaped damage, adding the caveat that personnel had been unable to access the site to carry out a full inspection. ESA confirmed that all of its personnel were safe and accounted for, although a number of staff remained directly affected by “restrictions on access to their homes and concerns for family members.” The Cebreros ground station is located approximately 77 kilometres west of Madrid and is one of ESA’s three deep-space ground stations. candidates.title: Juno reveals surprising subsurface tempertures at Io, remarkably smooth surface
candidates.raw_excerpt: Following two flybys of Jupiter’s innermost Galilean moon Io, teams using data from NASA’s Juno spacecraft have revealed the first measurements of the temperature below Io’s surface. The flybys revealed substantial subsurface heating on the moon, as well as a surface that is extremely smooth and composed of low-density materials. Io is the most volcanically active celestial body in the solar system, a characteristic caused by the immense tidal forces from its parent planet. As Io orbits Jupiter, the planet’s extreme gravity stretches and squeezes Io’s surface, generating an internal heat output significantly greater than that of Earth’s. However, until these new measurements, everything about Io’s thermal nature was learned through infrared observations of its surface. To make the subsurface temperature measurements, Juno used its Microwave Radiometer (MWR) instrument. Designed to make observations deep into Jupiter’s thick atmosphere, the MWR is multi-wavelength, supporting radiation observations from 1.3 cm to 51 cm wavelengths (600 MHz to 22 GHz frequencies). MWR achieves these observations via six differently sized antennas mounted to the sides of Juno. The MWR has also conducted observations of Ganymede and Europa. MWR data map showing where heat is rising from Io’s subsurface environment. The colors represent a temperature gradient across Io. (Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/USGS) “The Juno Microwave Radiometer directly observed Io’s heat output by looking below the surface. The surprising discovery that we could see below a rocky moon’s surface has important implications for studying Earth’s volcanoes. Juno has taught us that if we look with an MWR-type instrument near a volcano on Earth, we might see a similar signature in the subsurface temperature gradient, providing new information on how terrestrial volcanoes work,” said co-author and Juno principal investigator Scott Bolton of the Southwest Research Institute. candidates.title: Father-Son Duo Accused of Kidnapping Government Biologists Who Were Out Studying Frogs
candidates.raw_excerpt: An expedition to study frog habitats in Northern California’s Shasta-Trinity National Forest was cut short last week, with a father-son duo accused of taking two federal biologists hostage. The pair, identified as Joseph Charles Henrichsen and his adult son Phoenix Henrichsen, have been charged with kidnapping two US forest service researchers at gunpoint, NBC reports . Using a semi-automatic rifle, the Henrichsens are alleged to have kidnapped the biologists on the morning of Thursday, July 16. The as-yet-unidentified researchers were reportedly zip-tied and held in a remote camper-trailer, while Joseph Henrichsen used a phone belonging to one of the biologists to contact authorities. “I’ve taken two fed biologists hostage from the Forest Service,” the senior Henrichsen allegedly said in a message, per an affidavit filed a week after the incident. “I’m driving in the ranger vehicle right now.” At one point, Joseph Henrichsen is said to have taken one of the workers, identified only as a woman, into the US forest service truck. “Her hands are behind her f***ing back, and I’ve got live rounds ready,” he said, before requesting to talk to a federal agent. Thankfully, negotiators were able to diffuse the horrifying situation without any bloodshed, as the duo released the captive biologists before surrendering at 1am last Friday, per NBC . Now, a week after the incident, the burning question seems to be why a father-son duo in the remote reaches of California would do such a thing. So far, court documents don’t list any possible motives, and a spokesperson for the US attorney’s office prosecuting the case told NBC they’re “not able to go beyond what is included in that filing.” One possible explanation: the father and son could have been two of the state’s many anti-government extremists. candidates.title: Meta Is Letting Fake AI-Generated Doctors Sell Quack Cures on Its Platforms
candidates.raw_excerpt: Fake AI-generated doctors and health gurus have taken over Facebook and Instagram, sharing unproven medical advice and peddling dubious supplements. A recent New York Times investigation into the phenomenon reviewed hundreds of these ads, finding that they tend to follow a loose formula to draw people in. The AI videos usually feature AI avatars that present themselves as credible figures like doctors or Eastern medical gurus. Many prominently feature American flags or are set in familiar suburban settings. Some of the AI avatars are made to look like average people who’re really enthusiastic about the supplement they’re taking, filming themselves in a parking lot, bedroom, or grocery store — not unlike human influencers. The doctor avatars, meanwhile, might be in an office, where their fake diplomas are clearly on display. (One bears the incredible text “University of Degree” in a video identified by the NYT .) “In Chinese medicine, we have known exactly how to bring this down for generations,” says one AI-generated Asian grandma dressed in a labcoat highlighted in the investigation. Many of the claims these videos make are misleading and outright dangerous. One advertising a product called “Sculptique” asserts that taking its herbal supplement treats kidney disease better than medication. The company claims it gave 100 people with stage three kidney disease its supplement, showing an AI-generated video of these fake recipients raising their supplement bottles together in a warehouse. A 71-year-old named Pamela Wundrow told the NYT that she bought a supplement called moringa to treat her symptoms related to autoimmune disease after seeing ads for it on Facebook from a company called Rosabella.  Months after she started taking the pills daily, federal regulators announced a recall for Rosabella’s moringa supplement because some of its contaminated pills were sickening people with salmonella. candidates.title: Meta Desperately Trying to Ban Creeps Misusing Its AI “Pervert Glasses”
candidates.raw_excerpt: Meta’s camera-equipped AI glasses have quickly turned into a massively controversial accessory. They’ve been used by all kinds of charlatans and brutes to harass strangers, from pickup artist “ manfluencers ” filming themselves approaching strangers to juvenile pranksters recording members of the public without their consent. Consequently, the backlash to Meta’s “ pervert glasses ” has reached a fever pitch, with owners choosing to leave them at home to avoid embarrassment . Sensing a threat to its bottom line, Meta has slowly started treating the issue with some degree of seriousness. Now it’s vowing to crack down on creeps misusing its allegedly “privacy-first” glasses, as Business Insider reports : in an Instagram story, the platform’s head Adam Mosseri said the company would ban any user uploading videos showing them harassing others. “If you’re posting content that is taking advantage of people and harassing them, like a lot of these pickup line kind of videos that we’ve heard of and seen, then we’re going to take the content down,” he said. “We don’t want people to be surreptitiously taking videos of other people and harassing them and then posting them on our platform. So we’re trying to fight that every way we can.” According to BI , two large pickup artist accounts on Instagram have been deactivated. A spokesperson later confirmed that the accounts were banned for posting harassing content filmed with the glasses. Take it all together, and it’s one of the clearest indications yet that Meta is struggling to control the narrative about how its flashy glasses are being used by the public. The eyewear’s concealed cameras, in particular, have sparked a thorny debate over privacy and consent. It remains trivially easy to record somebody in public with them without their knowledge. candidates.title: Scientists Discover Massive Alien “Exosatellite”
candidates.raw_excerpt: Scientists have discovered a puzzling object in a distant star system that defies classification. Hear us out. The object in question orbits a brown dwarf. A brown dwarf is a substellar type of object that larger than a gas giant but smaller than the smallest stars. And this brown dwarf, in turn, orbits the system’s main star. Since the newly-identified object doesn’t orbit a planet, it technically isn’t a “moon” by any normal definition, but it’s not clearly a planet either, making its classification elusive. “This system is somewhat hard to define using Solar-System-based words like ‘planet’ and ‘moon,'” said European Southern Observatory (ESO) student Kevin Hoy, lead author of a new study published in the journal Nature , in a statement . “More than 6,000 exoplanets being discovered, no exomoon has ever been confidently detected,” Hoy and his colleagues noted in the paper. “Although there are candidates, they lack confirmation and remain controversial.” “This is the first time, to our knowledge, this technique has produced evidence of satellites around a companion brown dwarf,” the paper continues. The system’s main star, CD-35 2722, is roughly half the mass of our Sun and is located around 72 light-years from our solar system. Hoy and his colleagues are now trying to come up with a new label for the strange object. One moniker that has stuck is “exosatellite,” an object with at least the mass of Jupiter, while the brown dwarf has more than 30 times the mass of the gas giant. “The exosatellite is clearly massive enough to be a planet, but it does not orbit a star, though it orbits an object that orbits a star,” Hoy explained in the statement. “Being the third wheel in this system makes us want to call it a moon, even if it is nothing like the small, rocky moons we have in our system.” “We have a clear delineation between the planets and the Sun in the Solar System, so defining things like moons is simple,” added the paper’s coauthor and Universidad Diego Portales

candidates.title: Bryan Johnson Says He’s Cloned Himself “As a Newborn” to “Grow Organs for Transplantation,” Which Is a Preposterous Exaggeration
candidates.raw_excerpt: Zillionaire eccentric Bryan Johnson, fresh off of being diagnosed with an incurable disease , says he just “cloned” himself “as a newborn.” Yep, you heard that right. The immortality influencer shared in an X update that he has a “baby” version of himself growing in a petri dish that he says will allow him to become his “own blood boy” — doesn’t he already have a son who does that for him ? — and potentially even “grow organs for transplantation.” “This may be scary to some people… a dystopian future,” Johnson wrote. “But, for others, they will see it as the inevitable future of health.” In case this is all starting to sound like the grim sci-fi plot of a certain Michael Bay movie or Kazuo Ishiguro novel, it’s not a literal, living breathing clone. (Although by posting an infamous picture of himself edited to look like a baby, Johnson’s certainly playing into that impression.) Instead, Johnson’s created his own pluripotent stem cells . These stem cells can self-renew and develop into any type of cell in the body, making them invaluable for repairing damaged tissue.  Where Johnson’s claims of cloning himself as a “newborn” come in is the fact that these highly versatile stem cells normally only exist when we’re still an embryo. But in recent decades scientists have developed techniques to reprogram regular adult cells into an embryonic pluripotent state, which are called induced pluripotent stem cells. Johnson is confident that by having his own store of stem cells on hand he can “rebuild” his body, repairing everything from damaged lungs to eyesight. “This technology gives us a path to reverse aging,” he declares. His optimism is admirable, but many of these stem cell applications he’s touting haven’t been proven yet. Johnson claims his baby clone will let him grow organs, for example, but scientists still haven’t developed a reliable technique for creating organs derived from someone’s own stem cells . candidates.title: Man Accused of Horrific Crimes Caught Hiding as Pharma Executive
candidates.raw_excerpt: For over two decades, a notorious fugitive accused of horrible crimes in Rhode Island hid out in one of the places you’d most expect — the corner office of a Big Pharma company. Reported by Stat News , a 70-year old chief medical officer at the California-based firm Immix Biopharma was found to be afugitive sex predator who disappeared during his 2005 trial. Though he went by Richard Graydon in the more than twenty years since, his real name turns out to be Ronald Fischer — an anesthesiologist accused of raping numerous women on his various yachts (yes, plural). “Although I believe my trial has gone very well and expect to be acquitted and dismissed, the small chance of losing could carry extremely and unacceptably harsh penalties,” Fischer told his lawyer via email before fleeing in 2005. “I have therefore decided not to take the risk and leave the US and enjoy life in another country where I have long been carefully planning a good, safe, secure and comfortable life.” As it happens, Fischer never left for another country — at least not for good — but restarted his medical career in the US, leading him to rack up a number of aliases. Refusing to abandon his yachts or the medical career that paid for them, Fischer reportedly worked his way through a number of biotech companies, like Atossa Therapeutics, which appointed him interim chief medical officer in 2022. After being hired by Immix in March of 2026, Fischer was arrested after US Marshals boarded his 56-foot vessel, The Silver Lining , as it sailed down New York’s East River. While it remains to be seen how he evaded authorities for so long, if there’s any real silver lining, it’s that this horrible fugitive is no longer lurking around the Biotech sector, or society at large. candidates.raw_excerpt: Robotics company Realbotix LLC has long struggled to beat the allegations that its voluptuous humanoid robots are designed with prurient interests in mind. Yet the company has insisted she’s not a sex doll, leading to plenty of incredulity online. Adding to the drama is the company’s corporate structure: Realbotix LLC is owned by Realbotix Corp, which also owns Intima LLC — a venture that holds an ownership stake in Realdoll , one of the best-known manufacturers of sex robots. The AI-enabled robot would reportedly serve as a teaching assistant for high school students enrolled in STEM and arts courses. It’s hard not to see the company’s sex robot roots in Sally’s visage. The $57,000 android has smooth silicone skin , a dazed expression on her face, and an ill-fitting wig made of long brown hair. But after this story was first published, an attorney representing Realbotix reached out to emphasize what he said was a total divide between Realbotix LLC and Intima LLC. “Realbotix Corp is a holding company with two separately operated businesses: Realbotix LLC, which focuses on AI-powered humanoid robotics for commercial service sector applications, and Intima LLC, which focuses on direct-to-consumer products,” the attorney said, in a statement echoing a press release the company issued last week. “Realbotix LLC and Intima LLC have different product offerings with no crossover. candidates.title: Eminent Domain Could Be Used to Seize Your Land for AI Data Centers
candidates.raw_excerpt: Can companies seize your private property to build data center infrastructure?  According to legal scholar Aaron Walayat at the University of Dayton, it’s certainly a possibility. In a new piece for The Conversation , Walayat warns that power companies in states like George and Pennsylvania have been considering the use of eminent domain — the government’s prerogative to seize land without its owners’ consent — to build more transmission lines used to power data centers. If a landowner refuses a power company’s payout, the power company can turn to the local government to seize the land if it’s for “public use,” paying the landowner “just compensation.” These seizures are called condemnations, and most of the time they’re carried out by state and local governments, according to Walayat. In the case of transmission lines, the power company would be able to buy an easement on the landowner’s property. But so-called “common carriers” like power and water companies can exercise this power too, he added, if governments delegate it. And while many states have placed heavy restrictions on how condemnations are used, courts have typically allowed entities like utilities and power companies to exercise it. They’ve even allowed homes to be demolished in the name of “public use” and economic development. In 2005, the US Supreme Court sided with the the city of New London, Connecticut, allowing it to seize homes to build a private development around a Pfizer facility. But that development never materialized, and this lead to 45 states passing stricter eminent domain reform laws, Walayat noted. Any condemnations for transmission lines will face plenty of legal challenges, but aren’t without precedent. Walayat says that the supreme courts of South Dakota and Vermont have both backed up seizures by power companies, on the grounds that their transmission lines provided some energy to in-state customers and shored-up their local power-grid. candidates.title: Startup Sued After Delivery Bot Clobbers 73-Year Old Woman
candidates.raw_excerpt: With so many landmark lawsuits emerging around artificial intelligence, it can be easy to lose sight of the other high-tech cases shaping the world as we know it. One major suit with important implications just emerged out of Phoenix. The case revolves around a 2023 incident involving a 73-year-old named Trudy Perez and a delivery robot at Arizona State University. The woman — who was working as a parking garage attendant at the time — alleges a delivery robot operated by the company Starship Technologies repeatedly ran into her, throwing her to the ground and clobbering her again while she was down. Now, the woman is proceeding with a civil suit targeting Starship for liability and negligence, local station KJZZ reported . As if working outdoors in Phoenix at the age of 73 isn’t rough enough, a police report from the incident notes Perez suffered a four-inch gash on her arm as a result of the beat-down, in addition to back pain and mobility problems. Per KJZZ , she’s now seeking compensatory damages related to medical expenses, pain and suffering, and lost wages caused by the altercation. The lawsuit further alleges that, like similar automated robots , the experimental Starship unit was being piloted by an off-site employee. Per the filing, this unnamed employee neglected to “exercise control” over the delivery bot throughout the incident, resulting in Perez’s injuries. Of course, the company is doing everything it can to soften the blow and limit its liability. As KJZZ reports, Starship Technologies has a laundry list of excuses: not only were Perez’s injuries caused by her own negligence, but they were pre-existing as well, the company’s attorneys claim. With the first court date set for next February, it’ll be some time before the jury reaches a verdict. When they do, they could set some major precedent when it comes to holding companies responsible for mayhem caused by their delivery robots — an increasingly important issue as the gadgets spread to more cities
